hits.text:
Anthropic pointed a model at 40 years of ribosome papers and it found the same experiment had been run 1,400 times without anyone noticing.

Nobody asked it for a discovery. It was asked one question: which of these results has never been reproduced by a different lab.

> INGEST - 40 years of papers, methods sections only, no abstracts, no citations
> STRIP - reduces each method to the actual procedure, discarding how it was written up
> MATCH - clusters procedures that are the same experiment under different names
> ORPHAN - flags every cluster where one lab is the only source
> RANK - sorts orphans by how much later work was built on top of them

1,400 duplicates were harmless. Everyone re-runs the standard assays, and that is how science is supposed to work.

The output that mattered was the opposite pile. 61 procedures with exactly one source, each cited hundreds of times.

Four of those 61 sit underneath entire subfields, and no second lab has ever run the experiment.

Citations are not replication. A paper cited 900 times has been read 900 times, which is not the same as being checked once.

The literature is searchable by words and by authors. Almost nobody has indexed it by procedure, which is the only unit that can actually be repeated.

A reproducibility audit is a grant, a committee and two years. This was a weekend of compute against text that was already public.

How it's wired is in the article below.

THIS EXACT STACK PAYS ME $11,000+ EVERY MONTH

→ YouTube does not demonetise AI. It demonetises sameness. Their policy targets mass-produced templated content, and it names "visualising a character and a narrative you invented" as a legitimate use. The line is originality, not tooling.

A 22-year-old photographer from Tromsø borrowed her roommate's mason jar and disappeared into the snow for an hour. She wouldn't say why.

By the next morning, her 12-second clip had reached 3 million views.

Her plan was simple: capture the northern lights in a glass jar. not a photo of them. the actual aurora. in a jar. held in her hands. glowing.

The clip: a snowy forest road at night. tire tracks. footprints. aurora borealis rippling green and purple across the sky. a small flame of aurora light hovers above the path. hands reach out with a mason jar and scoop it up. the aurora ribbon sits inside the glass, swirling. green light reflects off the snow and off her fingers.

She didn't invent a new trend. She borrowed the "catch impossible nature in a container" format that was already working and applied it to the one natural phenomenon every traveler wants to hold.

The $29 went to a Seedance 2.5 subscription.

She typed one sentence, hit generate, and walked outside to watch the real aurora while the fake one rendered.

Then she ran the system again: different location, different aurora color, same jar.

One character she can keep building around. One format she can reuse every clear night for the rest of winter.

Find out how to do it in the article below

you can use jev for free now, and after a week on it i'm not going back

a 24-year-old is clearing $11,300 a month making "impossible renovation" clips. no house. no tools. no building permit.

Total setup cost: $29/month.
Render speed: 5 minutes per clip.
Rooms renovated: ZERO.

HIS SYSTEM WORKS LIKE THIS:

> PICK an impossible material: 10,000 mini pumpkins, crushed gemstones, bottle caps, seashells, Skittles
> DUMP a mountain of it in a white room. one guy in blue overalls with a rake.
> CUT TO: two workers grinding the pile into a smooth resin floor with industrial polishers
> REVEAL: a flawless, glossy floor made entirely of the impossible material. reflections perfect.
> POST as "DIY floor made of [material]" and watch the renovation community lose its mind

this week's clip: thousands of green and orange mini pumpkins piled in a white room. a man rakes them flat. two workers grind the surface with floor polishers. the pumpkins compress into a smooth, glossy terrazzo-like floor.

1. GPT-6 Astra: writes the material list, room dimensions, and grinding sequence: 3 min
2. Seedream: generates 42 reference frames of the room, pile, and finished floor: 10 min
3. Seedance 2.5: animates the raking, grinding, and polishing with correct tool vibration and material compression: 20 min
4. Cartesia: grinder motor hum, pumpkin crush, and the satisfying final polish sweep: auto
5. Picsart: speed ramp from pile to finished floor, vertical export: 5 min

the format is infinitely repeatable. new material, same white room, same overalls, same reveal.

$11,300 a month, five tools, zero floors he ever built.

the full build is in the article.

A group of Chinese students from Stanford University published an architecture where an agent saying "done" means nothing. only evidence can mark a task complete.

three layers:

> graph engineering controls states and transitions. no verification evidence, no transition.

> loop engineering owns failure: diagnose, repair, retry, re-verify. up to 20 attempts under hard time, token, cost and tool budgets.

> the zero-trust harness authorizes every action, isolates execution and writes audit evidence for every path.

they tested it across 3,360 executions.

verified completion: 56.4% -> 95.0%
recovery success: 51.0% -> 93.1%
evidence-gated execution: 100%
unauthorized capability denial: 140/140
bounded termination: 100%

even when the model fails, the framework never lets an unsupported success through.

models decide how well.
the harness decides whether.

last november japan simulated the milky way star by star for the first time in history. 300 billion particles. 7,630,848 cpu cores. a billion dollar machine pulling 30 megawatts, the power of a small town. the old way, that single run needed 36 years of compute. i had to read that twice

This is the whole architecture of an AI agent, written down by Anthropic

The piece is called Building effective agents, and it starts by splitting two things people keep mixing up.

A workflow is a system where the path is written in code. You decided the order, the model fills in the steps.

An agent is a system where the model directs its own process and keeps control of how the task gets done.

Then it names the pieces. The augmented LLM, a model given retrieval, tools and memory, is the block everything else is built from. 

On top of it sit five workflows: prompt chaining, routing, parallelization, orchestrator-workers, evaluator-optimizer. Past those, the autonomous agent running a loop with its environment.

The finding that matters: the teams shipping this successfully were not using frameworks. 

Simple composable patterns, and complexity added only where it measurably helped.

The fish picks it up, swims over to the merchant and gets an offer:

$1.28.

Obviously, that's not enough.

So the fish grabs the merchant by the head and suddenly the offer becomes $1.73.

Negotiations are going well.

But then I realized the fish should be able to trade more than random items.

So I added the humans it catches to the same world.

Now the fish can go back to the seabed, pick up its catch and bring it straight to the merchant's table.

The merchant doesn't seem particularly prepared for this business model.

This is slowly turning into an actual game now.

You fish for humans, collect things from the underwater world, trade your loot and interact with whatever strange creatures are running the economy down there.

And I already have more mechanics planned.

The ocean is getting a lot more interesting.
